title: What Is Reecap? The Online Video Editor and Motion Design Tool, Explained
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Reecap is two creative tools in one browser tab: a photo-to-video recap editor and a layer-by-layer Motion Design studio. Here is everything it does, who it is for, and how the two tools work together.
description: A complete guide to Reecap, the free browser-based video editor and motion design tool. Learn what it does, how the two tools work, and how to make animated videos with no install and no account.

body.text: Reecap is a free, browser-based studio for turning visuals into motion. It bundles two tools that most creators normally need separate apps for: a photo-to-video recap editor and a layer-by-layer Motion Design tool. Both run entirely in your browser tab, with no install, no sign-up, and nothing uploaded to a server. If you have ever wanted to make a polished recap of your week, or animate a flat design into something that stops the scroll, Reecap is built to do both from the same place.

This guide is the full picture: what each tool does, who Reecap is for, how the pieces fit together, and the realistic limits you should know before you start. By the end you will understand exactly where Reecap fits in your workflow and how to get a finished result fast.
The one-sentence version

Reecap turns photos into a shareable MP4, and turns designs into animations, all inside your browser. That is the whole promise. Everything below is just detail on how it delivers that promise without the friction of desktop software.
Tool one: the video recap editor

The recap editor is the original heart of Reecap. You drop in a batch of photos, arrange them on a real timeline, and the editor strings them into a cinematic video with transitions, captions, and music. It is the fastest way to turn a camera roll into something worth posting.

What makes it more than a basic slideshow maker is control. Every slide can have its own duration and its own transition. You are not locked into one global style applied to everything. A montage can snap quickly through a dozen shots, then linger on the one that matters, then ease into the next chapter. That per-slide control is what separates a video that feels intentional from one that feels automated.

The transitions themselves are genuinely cinematic rather than cheesy. You get fade, slide, slide-up, zoom, wipe, flip, dissolve, and a clean cut, and you can mix them across a single project. Captions are a first-class feature too: you can drop text on any slide, drag it anywhere on the canvas, recolor it, add a background pill for legibility, and animate it in with a fade, pop, slide, or typewriter effect.

items: Per-slide duration and transition, not one global setting
Eight transition styles you can mix in a single video
Draggable, recolorable, animated captions on any slide
A whole-video speed dial from a gentle 0.5x up to a 10x blur
Background music from a built-in library that plays across the recap
Aspect ratios for every platform: 16:9, 9:16, 1:1, 4:3, and 5:4

body.text: When you are happy, you export a real MP4. Reecap composites every frame at 30 frames per second using WebCodecs, the browser's hardware-accelerated media engine. That means the transitions, caption animations, and music are all baked into the file, not just shown in a preview. You can pick 720p or 1080p, and the finished video downloads straight to your device with no watermark.
Tool two: the Motion Design studio

The newer tool is where Reecap stops being a slideshow maker and becomes a design tool. Motion Design is a layer-based animation studio in the spirit of apps like Jitter or After Effects, but built for the browser and for people who do not want to learn a complex timeline of keyframes.

You start with a canvas and add layers: text, rectangles, ellipses, and images. Each layer can be positioned, resized, rotated, and recolored directly on the canvas, exactly as you would expect from a design tool. Then you give each layer an animation. This is the part that feels different: instead of manually setting keyframes, you pick a preset for how the layer enters and how it leaves.

The presets cover the moves you actually use every day: fade, slide in any direction, scale, pop, blur, and rotate. Each one has an easing curve, including spring and bounce, so the motion feels natural instead of robotic. You set when a layer starts, how long its entrance takes, and how long its exit takes, and the engine handles the in-between. A timeline at the bottom shows each layer as a clip you can drag to move and resize to change timing.

items: Add text, shape, and image layers on an infinite-feeling canvas
Drag, resize, rotate, and recolor every layer
Keyframe-free in and out animation presets with real easing
Group layers so they move and animate together
A draggable, zoomable timeline with resizable clips
Reorder layers with a right-click menu and keyboard shortcuts

body.text: How the two tools connect

You switch between the video editor and Motion Design with a single toggle in the header, or from the sidebar menu. They share the same workspace, the same theme, and the same export-minded philosophy. The idea is that one tab can take you from raw photos to a finished recap, or from a flat design to a moving graphic, without ever leaving the browser or learning a second interface.

The bridge that makes Motion Design especially powerful for designers is Figma import. Reecap ships a companion Figma plugin: you select a frame in Figma, click a button, and the frame is copied to your clipboard. Paste it into Reecap's Motion canvas and it arrives as an editable frame with its text, shapes, groups, and colors intact. You are not pasting a flat screenshot. You are pasting a real, editable layer tree you can immediately animate.
Who Reecap is for

Reecap is built for people who want a professional result without a professional learning curve. That includes social media creators making Reels and Shorts, marketers building quick ad creatives and promos, small business owners who cannot justify a designer for every post, educators turning lessons into engaging clips, and designers who want to animate a screen without booting up After Effects.

It is especially good for the person who has a great visual but no motion skills. If you can drag a box and pick from a menu, you can make something move. The presets do the hard part, which is making the motion feel good rather than mechanical.
What makes Reecap different

Three things set Reecap apart from the crowd of online video makers. First, it is genuinely browser-native. There is no desktop app to install, no render farm to wait on, and no account wall to cross before you can try it. Second, it is private by design. Because the recap editor renders on your own machine with WebCodecs, your photos never leave your device. There are no servers handling your media, no analytics on your content, and nothing left behind when you close the tab. Third, it combines editing and motion design in one place, which almost no free tool does.

items: No download, no account, no upload step
Runs and renders on your own device for true privacy
Two tools in one: video editing plus motion design
Free and open source, exporting watermark-free MP4s
Installable as a progressive web app that launches into the editor

body.text: The honest limits

Being straight with you matters more than overselling. The video editor's MP4 export is fully working today. The Motion Design tool is newer, and exporting a motion project to video is still rolling out, so for now Motion is the place you design, preview, and refine animations. Figma import reconstructs text, shapes, frames, and groups, but custom fonts fall back to a system font and complex vector or effect-heavy nodes come in as flattened images rather than fully editable vectors. None of this stops you from doing real work; it just sets the right expectations.
How to get started in five minutes

Open the editor, and you are immediately in the video tool. Drag in a handful of photos, and they appear on the canvas and timeline. Set a transition, add a caption, pick a track from the music library, and press play to preview. When it looks right, hit Export and choose 1080p. In under five minutes you have a shareable MP4.

To try motion, flip the header toggle to Motion. Add a text layer and a rectangle, give each one a slide or pop preset, and press play to watch them animate in. If you design in Figma, install the Reecap Motion plugin, copy a frame, and paste it in to see your real design land on the canvas, ready to bring to life.
Real workflows Reecap replaces

It helps to see where Reecap slots into real life rather than in the abstract. A travel creator who used to wrestle a phone app for an hour can drop a trip's photos into the recap editor, set transitions, drop in music, and export a polished clip in minutes. A founder announcing a launch can paste the product screen from Figma into Motion and have an animated teaser instead of a flat image. A teacher can turn a lesson's key points into an animated title sequence that holds a class's attention better than a static slide ever would.

The common thread is collapse: tasks that used to require a separate app, a separate skill set, or a separate person now happen in one tab. That collapse is the real product. It is not that Reecap does any single thing no other tool can; it is that it does the things most people actually need, in the place they already are, without the friction that usually stops a good idea from becoming a finished post.

items: Camera roll to shareable MP4 without a phone app
Figma frame to animated teaser without After Effects
Lesson points to an animated title card without a designer
Product shots to a promo clip without a video editor on staff

body.text: If your work involves turning visuals into something people watch, there is a good chance one of these workflows is yours. The fastest way to know is to try it: the editor is one click away, and the first result takes about five minutes.
The bottom line

Reecap is the rare tool that respects both your time and your privacy. It gives a beginner the power to make something that looks intentional, and it gives a designer a fast lane from a static frame to motion. Whether you are recapping a trip or animating a product screen, it is all one browser tab away, free to start, and yours to keep.

Ready to see it for yourself? Open the editor and start in the video tool: drag in a few photos, pick a transition, add a caption, and export a clean MP4 in about five minutes. Then flip the header toggle to Motion, drop in a text layer and a shape, give each one a preset, and press play to watch them animate. If you design in Figma, install the Reecap Motion plugin and paste a frame to feel the whole loop end to end. Nothing here requires a sign-up, a download, or a single thing leaving your device, so the only cost of trying is a few minutes of curiosity. The best way to understand a tool that does two jobs in one tab is simply to do one of them, and the first finished result is usually the moment it clicks into place for good.

faq.q: Is Reecap free?
faq.a: Yes. Reecap is free and open source. There is no account to create, and you can export watermark-free MP4s from the video editor at no cost.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. Reecap runs in your browser. You can optionally install it as a progressive web app so it launches straight into the editor, but it is not required.

faq.q: Are my photos uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The recap editor processes and renders everything on your own device using the browser's WebCodecs engine. Your media never leaves your machine.

faq.q: What is the difference between the two tools?
faq.a: The video editor turns photos into a cinematic MP4 with transitions, captions, and music. The Motion Design tool animates individual layers of text, shapes, and images, and can import editable frames from Figma.

faq.q: Can I import my Figma designs?
faq.a: Yes. The companion Reecap Motion Figma plugin copies a selected frame; paste it into the Motion canvas and it arrives as an editable frame with its text, shapes, groups, and colors intact.

title: How to Animate Your Figma Designs Without After Effects
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: You designed a beautiful screen in Figma. Now make it move. This is the full, beginner-friendly workflow for turning a static Figma frame into an animation, using Reecap's Motion tool and its Figma plugin.
description: A step-by-step guide to animating Figma designs without After Effects. Learn how to copy a frame with the Reecap plugin, paste it as editable layers, and animate text, shapes, and groups with presets.

body.text: Figma is where the design lives, but Figma frames do not move. To get a shareable animation, most designers reach for After Effects, learn a wall of keyframes and expressions, and burn an afternoon on something that should take minutes. This guide shows the shorter path: copy a frame from Figma, paste it into Reecap's Motion tool as editable layers, and animate it with presets. No keyframe graphs, no plugins to render, no desktop install.

The result is the kind of layered, intentional motion you see in good product launch posts and onboarding clips: a card slides up, a headline fades in, a button pops, an icon spins into place. You will be able to build that in a single browser tab.
What you need before you start

You need three things: the Figma desktop app, the Reecap Motion plugin installed in Figma, and the Reecap web app open in your browser. The plugin is the bridge that carries your design out of Figma with its structure intact. Without it, the best you can do is paste a flat screenshot, which is not editable. With it, you paste a real layer tree.
Step 1: Install the Reecap Motion plugin

In the Figma desktop app, open the Plugins menu, choose Development, and import the plugin from its manifest. Once it is registered, it appears in your plugins list as Reecap Motion. You only do this once. The plugin reads the frame you have selected and prepares it for the trip to the browser.

A quick note on why a plugin is necessary: Figma's clipboard does not natively hand other web apps an editable copy of your design. The plugin walks the selected frame, classifies every node, and packages a compact description of the layer tree that Reecap knows how to rebuild.
Step 2: Select a frame and copy it

In Figma, click the frame you want to animate. Pick a real, self-contained frame such as a card, a hero section, a mobile screen, or a feature block. Run the Reecap Motion plugin. It shows a preview of your frame and a Copy to Reecap button. Click it. Your design is now on the clipboard as an editable payload, not a picture.

The plugin handles the messy parts for you. Text nodes are captured as editable text with their size, weight, color, and alignment. Rectangles and ellipses with solid fills become editable shapes with their corner radius. Frames and groups become real groups, so the nesting you built in Figma survives. Anything it cannot represent natively, like a complex vector icon or an image fill, is flattened to an image so it still looks right.
Step 3: Paste into Reecap's Motion canvas

Switch to Reecap in your browser and toggle to the Motion tool in the header. Click on the canvas and paste with Command-V or Control-V. Your frame appears exactly as it looked in Figma, but now it is made of layers you can touch. The composition resizes to match your frame, and the frame's background color carries over too.

Crucially, the frame lands as one tidy, collapsed group in the layers panel rather than a pile of loose layers. That keeps the panel clean. Expand the frame when you want to reach the text, shapes, and nested groups inside it. Everything is visible and static at first, just like the original design, so you can confirm it pasted correctly before you animate anything.
Step 4: Plan the motion before you touch a preset

Good motion is choreography, not chaos. Before animating, decide the order things should appear. A reliable pattern for a product card is: the container or background comes in first, then the headline, then supporting text, then the call-to-action button, then any decorative icon. This staggered entrance guides the eye down the design the same way a reader naturally scans it.

Think in terms of a short story with a beginning, a hold, and an end. Most social clips are two to six seconds. That is enough time for three or four elements to enter, hold long enough to be read, and optionally exit. Resist the urge to animate every single layer; motion is most powerful when a few key elements move and the rest stay calm.
Step 5: Animate each layer with presets

Select a layer, open the inspector, and find the Animate In section. Pick a preset. For the headline, a slide-up reads as confident and clean. For a button, a pop with a spring easing feels tactile and inviting. For a background card, a gentle scale or fade keeps it from competing with the content on top of it. Set the start time so each layer enters a beat after the previous one, and adjust the duration so nothing feels rushed or sluggish.

items: Use slide-up or fade for headlines and body text
Use pop with spring easing for buttons and badges
Use scale or fade for background cards and containers
Stagger start times by a fraction of a second for a cascade
Keep most layers still; let two or three carry the motion

body.text: Step 6: Use groups to move things together

Because your Figma frame imported as groups, you can animate a whole section at once. Select a group and give it a slide-in, and every layer inside it travels together while keeping its internal layout. This is the secret to fast, cohesive motion: animate the group for the big move, then add small individual accents to one or two children inside it for polish.
Step 7: Refine on the timeline

The timeline at the bottom shows each layer as a clip. Drag a clip to shift when it appears. Drag its edges to lengthen or shorten how long it is on stage. Zoom in for fine control or hit Fit to see the whole composition at once. Scrub the playhead to check any single moment, and press the spacebar to play the whole sequence. This is where a good animation becomes a great one: you are tuning the rhythm until the entrances land on the beat you imagined.
Step 8: Recolor and tweak without going back to Figma

Because the layers are editable, you do not have to return to Figma for small changes. Click a shape to change its fill. Click the frame group to change its background. Double-click text to rewrite it, or adjust its size and weight in the inspector. Want to test a louder accent color for the button? Change it in place and watch the animation again. This tight loop is what makes Reecap feel like a design tool rather than a converter.
Common mistakes and how to avoid them

The most common mistake is animating everything at once, which creates visual noise. Pick a hierarchy and let it breathe. The second mistake is making durations too short; a 0.2-second entrance reads as a flicker, while 0.5 to 0.8 seconds feels deliberate. The third is forgetting easing; a linear move feels robotic, so lean on ease-out, spring, or bounce to give motion a sense of weight.

items: Do not animate every layer; choose a clear hierarchy
Avoid ultra-short durations that read as a flicker
Always apply easing instead of leaving motion linear
Stagger entrances rather than firing them simultaneously
Hold each element on screen long enough to be read

body.text: What about fonts and complex graphics?

Set expectations here so nothing surprises you. Text content, size, weight, color, and alignment all transfer, but the exact custom typeface falls back to a system font in the browser, because a web tool cannot embed every Figma font. Solid-fill shapes and frames are fully editable. Vectors, icons, gradients, and effect-heavy nodes arrive as flattened images, which means they look correct but are not vector-editable. For most launch posts and UI animations, this is more than enough; for pixel-perfect brand typography, plan to keep critical type as editable text and accept the system-font preview.
Why this beats the After Effects route for most people

After Effects is extraordinarily powerful and the right tool for high-end work. But for the everyday job of animating a UI screen or a marketing card, it is heavy: a large install, a steep keyframe learning curve, and a separate import-export dance to get your Figma art in. Reecap collapses that into copy, paste, and pick a preset. You trade a small amount of ceiling for an enormous amount of speed, and for most social and product motion, that trade is the right one.
A worked example: animating a pricing card

Let us make the abstract concrete with a card you have probably designed a hundred times: a pricing card with a plan name, a price, a list of features, and a call-to-action button. In Figma, this is a frame containing a few text layers, a button, and maybe a highlight badge. You have grouped the contents, named the layers, and you are ready to make it move.

Copy the frame with the plugin and paste it into Motion. Now choreograph it. The card container scales in first with an ease-out, establishing the stage. The plan name slides up a beat later, confident and clean. The price pops with a spring easing, because the price is the hero and the pop draws the eye straight to it. The feature list fades in next, each line entering just after the last so the viewer reads down the list naturally. Finally the button pops with spring easing as the last element, the clear destination once everything else has settled.

items: Card container: scale in with ease-out, establishes the stage
Plan name: slide up a beat later
Price: pop with spring easing, it is the hero
Feature lines: fade in one after another down the list
Button: pop last as the clear call to action

body.text: Press play and you have a pricing card that feels alive and guides the eye exactly where you want it. The whole sequence took a handful of preset choices and a little timeline tuning. That is the entire promise of this workflow: your design, already finished, given motion in minutes rather than hours.
Putting it all together

The whole workflow is short once it is familiar: install the plugin once, then copy a frame, paste it into Motion, plan the order, apply presets, group for big moves, and refine on the timeline. The first time might take fifteen minutes as you learn the layout. After that, animating a design becomes a five-minute task you can do between other work, which is exactly the point. Your designs deserve to move, and now they can without a single keyframe.

The real unlock is treating this as a habit rather than a one-off. The first animation you make from a Figma frame will feel like a small experiment; the tenth will feel like part of how you ship. Keep the plugin installed, keep a Reecap tab handy, and the next time you finish a design that is destined for a feed, give it sixty extra seconds of motion before you post it. That tiny addition, repeated, is what separates a portfolio of static frames from a body of work that moves, and it costs you almost nothing now that the keyframes are gone.

faq.q: Do I need After Effects to animate a Figma design?
faq.a: No. With Reecap's Motion tool you copy a frame using the Reecap Figma plugin, paste it as editable layers, and animate each layer with presets, all in the browser.

faq.q: Does my Figma frame stay editable after pasting?
faq.a: Yes. Text, solid-fill shapes, frames, and groups paste as editable layers. Complex vectors and effects arrive as flattened images, and custom fonts fall back to a system font.

faq.q: Will the frame paste as one object or many loose layers?
faq.a: It pastes as a single collapsed frame group with its layers nested inside, so the layers panel stays tidy. Expand the frame to edit individual layers.

faq.q: How long should a design animation be?
faq.a: Most social and product clips work best between two and six seconds, long enough for a few elements to enter, hold to be read, and optionally exit.

faq.q: Can I change colors after importing from Figma?
faq.a: Yes. You can recolor any shape, change the frame's background, and edit text directly in Reecap without returning to Figma.

title: Motion Design for Beginners: How to Animate Without Complex Keyframes
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Motion design has a reputation for being hard. It is not, if you skip the keyframe graphs and learn a few timeless principles. This is a beginner's guide to making things move well, with no prior experience.
description: A beginner's guide to motion design without keyframes. Learn the core principles of good animation, easing, timing, and hierarchy, and how to apply them with preset-based tools like Reecap.

body.text: Motion design looks intimidating from the outside. Open a tutorial and you are buried in keyframe graphs, bezier handles, and expressions within minutes. But here is the secret that experienced animators know: the keyframes are just the mechanics. The thing that actually makes motion look good is a small set of principles you can learn in an afternoon. This guide teaches those principles and shows how preset-based tools let you apply them without touching a single keyframe.

If you have ever thought you are not a motion person, this is for you. You do not need to be technical. You need to understand a few ideas about how things move in the real world, and then borrow them.
What motion design actually is

Motion design is the craft of moving graphic elements with intention. It is the headline that slides into place, the icon that pops as it is mentioned, the chart that draws itself, the logo that assembles. Unlike traditional video editing, which arranges footage, motion design animates designed elements: text, shapes, images, and UI. The goal is almost always the same: guide attention, add personality, and make information easier to absorb.
Principle 1: Easing is everything

If you remember one thing, remember this. Nothing in the real world moves at a constant speed. A ball that falls accelerates. A car that stops decelerates. When an element moves at a constant, linear speed, your brain reads it as fake and mechanical, even if you cannot say why. Easing is the curve that describes how a movement speeds up and slows down, and it is the single biggest difference between amateur and professional motion.

The two you will use most are ease-out and ease-in-out. Ease-out starts fast and slows into place; it feels responsive and is perfect for elements entering the screen. Ease-in-out starts slow, speeds up, and slows down; it feels smooth and natural for movement across the screen. Two more add character: spring overshoots slightly and settles, giving a lively, tactile feel that is great for buttons and badges; bounce makes an element land and rebound, which adds playful energy when used sparingly.

items: Linear: constant speed, reads as robotic, avoid for most motion
Ease-out: fast then slow, ideal for entrances
Ease-in-out: smooth on both ends, ideal for moving across screen
Spring: a gentle overshoot that feels alive and tactile
Bounce: lands and rebounds, playful when used in moderation

body.text: Principle 2: Timing and spacing

Timing is how long a movement takes; spacing is how far it travels in that time. Together they create the feel of weight. A heavy object moves slowly and with momentum; a light object snaps quickly. For UI and text, durations between 0.4 and 0.8 seconds usually feel right. Shorter than 0.2 seconds and the motion reads as a flicker the eye cannot follow. Longer than about a second and it starts to feel sluggish, like the interface is waiting on itself.
When in doubt, slightly slower with strong easing beats fast and linear. Give the viewer enough time to register the movement, but not so much that they get impatient.
Principle 3: Hierarchy and staggering

Everything moving at once is noise. The most reliable trick in all of motion design is the stagger: instead of firing every element simultaneously, you offset their start times by a fraction of a second so they cascade in sequence. This does two things. It guides the eye along a path you choose, and it turns a flat reveal into a rhythm that feels designed.

Decide what matters most and let it lead. In a typical layout, that means the container appears first, then the headline, then supporting text, then the call to action. Each element gets its moment. The viewer's eye is gently walked down the design exactly the way you want them to read it.
Principle 4: Restraint

Beginners tend to over-animate because every new effect is exciting. The mark of mature motion design is restraint. A composition where two or three elements move and the rest hold still feels confident and premium. A composition where everything spins, bounces, and slides feels frantic and cheap. Motion is seasoning, not the meal. Use it to emphasize, not to decorate every corner.
Principle 5: Enter, hold, exit

Think of every element's life on screen as three acts. It enters, it holds long enough to be read or understood, and it optionally exits. The hold is the part beginners forget. If a headline slides in and immediately slides out, no one can read it. The hold is where the message actually lands. For looping social clips, you might skip the exit entirely and let elements rest in their final state until the loop restarts.
How presets let you skip keyframes

Here is where modern tools change the game. In traditional software, you express all of the above by hand: you set a keyframe for the start position, another for the end, then bend the curve between them to get your easing. It works, but it is slow and fiddly. A preset-based tool like Reecap's Motion editor encodes these principles into named choices. You pick a slide-up entrance, choose a spring easing, set a start time and a duration, and the tool generates the correct motion for you. You are still making every important decision, you are just not doing the tedious math.

This is not a lesser form of animation. It is the same principles delivered faster. You think in terms of intention, the entrance should feel confident, the button should feel tactile, and you choose the preset that expresses that, rather than translating intention into bezier handles.
A first project you can try right now

Let us make a simple animated title card to put the principles into practice. Open Reecap and switch to the Motion tool. Add a rectangle for a background card and give it a gentle scale entrance with ease-out. Add a text layer for your headline and give it a slide-up entrance with a slightly later start time, so it follows the card. Add a second, smaller text layer for a subtitle, slide it up too, but a beat after the headline. Finally, add a small shape as an accent and give it a pop with spring easing as the last element to arrive.

items: Background card: scale in with ease-out, starts first
Headline: slide up, starts a beat after the card
Subtitle: slide up, starts a beat after the headline
Accent shape: pop with spring, arrives last for a flourish
Hold everything for a second before the loop restarts

body.text: Press play. You just built a staggered, eased, hierarchical animation, the exact same structure a professional would use, without setting a single keyframe. Tweak the start times until the cascade feels musical, and you have your first real piece of motion design.
Building taste over time

The principles get you to competent quickly. Taste comes from watching. Start paying attention to motion in the apps and ads you already use. Notice how a good app eases its transitions, how a strong ad staggers its text, how restraint makes premium brands feel premium. Try to name what you see: that was an ease-out slide, that was a spring pop, that was a staggered reveal. Once you can name it, you can reproduce it.
Common beginner traps

A few patterns will trip you up early. Animating with linear easing makes everything feel cheap; always reach for a curve. Making durations too fast turns motion into a flicker; slow down. Animating everything at once creates chaos; pick a hierarchy. Forgetting the hold means your message cannot be read; give elements time on stage. Avoid these four and you are already ahead of most beginners.
Secondary principles worth knowing

Once the five fundamentals feel natural, a few secondary ideas will sharpen your work further. Anticipation is a tiny preparatory move before the main action, the way you crouch slightly before jumping. A button that dips a hair before popping up feels more alive. Follow-through is the opposite end: things do not stop dead, they settle, which is exactly what spring and bounce easing give you for free. Overlap means not every part of an element moves in perfect lockstep; staggering even the pieces within a group adds richness.

Then there is consistency, which is less a motion principle than a design one but matters enormously. If every entrance in your piece uses the same easing and similar timing, the work feels intentional and cohesive. If each element moves to its own random rhythm, it feels chaotic even when each individual move is fine. Pick a motion language, a default easing, a default duration, a default entrance, and reuse it. Constraints make motion feel designed.

items: Anticipation: a small prep move before the main action
Follow-through: elements settle rather than stopping dead
Overlap: stagger the parts within a group for richness
Consistency: reuse the same easing and timing for cohesion

body.text: You do not need to master these on day one. They are the difference between motion that is good and motion that is polished, and they come naturally once the fundamentals are second nature. The point is that none of them require keyframe wizardry either; they are choices about timing and easing that a preset-based tool expresses just as well as a professional package.
The takeaway

Motion design is not about software wizardry. It is about understanding how things should move and then expressing that clearly. Easing, timing, hierarchy, restraint, and the enter-hold-exit rhythm are the whole foundation. With a preset-based tool, you can apply every one of them in minutes, no keyframes required. Start small, watch closely, and your motion will look intentional from your very first project.

If you take one action after reading this, let it be a tiny project tonight: open a motion tool, add three layers, and give each a staggered, eased entrance. That is it. The gap between thinking you are not a motion person and making something that genuinely moves well is smaller than it looks, and it closes the instant you build your first deliberate cascade. Principles plus a single hour of practice will take you further than weeks of watching tutorials without ever pressing play. Start small, watch the motion you admire with new eyes, and let your taste and your hands grow together.

faq.q: Do I need to learn keyframes to do motion design?
faq.a: No. Keyframes are just one way to express movement. Preset-based tools like Reecap's Motion editor let you apply professional easing, timing, and staggering by choosing named presets instead of setting keyframes by hand.

faq.q: What is easing and why does it matter?
faq.a: Easing is the curve that describes how a movement speeds up and slows down. Real objects never move at a constant speed, so easing is what makes motion feel natural instead of robotic. Ease-out, spring, and bounce are common choices.

faq.q: How long should an animation last?
faq.a: For text and UI elements, entrances of roughly 0.4 to 0.8 seconds feel right. Shorter reads as a flicker; much longer feels sluggish.

faq.q: Why does my animation look amateur?
faq.a: The usual culprits are linear easing, durations that are too fast, animating everything at once, and forgetting to hold elements on screen long enough to be read. Fixing those four issues makes a dramatic difference.

faq.q: What is a stagger?
faq.a: A stagger offsets the start times of multiple elements by a fraction of a second so they enter in sequence rather than all at once. It guides the eye and gives a reveal a designed rhythm.

title: Reecap vs After Effects: When the Browser Tool Is the Smarter Choice
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: After Effects is the industry standard, and that is exactly why it is overkill for most everyday motion. Here is an honest comparison of Reecap and After Effects, and how to choose the right tool for the job.
description: An honest comparison of Reecap and Adobe After Effects for motion design. See where each tool wins on speed, learning curve, cost, and output, and how to pick the right one for your project.

body.text: After Effects is the most powerful motion graphics tool ever made. It is also, for a huge number of the jobs people actually do, far more tool than the task requires. If your goal is to animate a UI screen, build a social post, or move a few text layers with style, reaching for After Effects can feel like renting a film studio to shoot a selfie. This comparison is an honest look at where Adobe's giant wins, where a browser tool like Reecap wins, and how to decide which one your project really needs.

To be clear up front: this is not a takedown of After Effects. It is the right tool for high-end, complex, frame-perfect work. The point is that most everyday motion is not that, and using the heaviest possible tool for a light job costs you time you do not get back.
The headline difference

After Effects is a professional desktop application with near-infinite depth: keyframes, expressions, 3D layers, plugins, particle systems, and an ecosystem two decades deep. Reecap is a browser-based motion tool built around presets, designed so that anyone can make good motion in minutes. One optimizes for ceiling; the other optimizes for speed and accessibility. Your project decides which one matters more.
Learning curve

This is the biggest practical gap. After Effects has a famously steep curve. Even basic tasks involve understanding compositions, layers, the keyframe model, easing graphs, and a dense interface. Most people need weeks of practice and a stack of tutorials before they feel competent, and longer before they feel fast. Reecap is built so that if you can use a design tool, you can animate. You add a layer, pick how it enters and leaves from a menu, and adjust timing on a simple timeline. The curve is measured in minutes, not weeks.
For a beginner, a marketer, or a designer who only occasionally needs motion, this difference is decisive. The best tool is the one you can actually use to finish the job today.
Speed to a finished result

For everyday motion, Reecap is dramatically faster. There is no app to launch, no project to set up, and no render queue. You open a tab, build, and preview instantly. Importing a design is a copy and paste away thanks to the Figma plugin. In After Effects, the same job involves launching the app, importing assets, recreating or relinking your design, keyframing each move, and then rendering out a file. For a quick post, that overhead can dwarf the actual creative work.

items: Reecap: open a tab, build, preview instantly, no setup
After Effects: launch, import, keyframe, render queue
Reecap pulls in Figma frames as editable layers by paste
After Effects requires importing and often rebuilding design art

body.text: Power and ceiling

This is where After Effects pulls firmly ahead, and it is not close. If you need complex 3D, particle effects, motion tracking, frame-by-frame character animation, advanced compositing, or precise control over every interpolation curve, After Effects does things Reecap simply does not attempt. For broadcast graphics, VFX, intricate explainer videos, and high-end brand work, the ceiling matters and Adobe owns it.

Reecap deliberately trades that ceiling for accessibility. Its preset model covers the moves most people use, fade, slide, scale, pop, blur, rotate, with real easing, plus grouping and a timeline. That is a complete toolkit for UI animation, social posts, and product motion, but it is not trying to be a VFX suite.
Cost

After Effects is a paid subscription, billed monthly or annually as part of Adobe's Creative Cloud. Over a year that adds up, and it never stops as long as you need the software. Reecap is free and open source. For an individual creator, a small business, a student, or anyone who only needs motion occasionally, the cost difference is significant. You can do real work in Reecap without a credit card.
Hardware and accessibility

After Effects is demanding. It wants a capable machine with a strong CPU, plenty of RAM, and ideally a good GPU, and renders can still tax it. Reecap runs in a browser, so it works on modest laptops and does not require a powerful workstation. It is also instantly accessible from any device with a modern browser, with nothing to install. For teams on mixed hardware or creators without a high-end machine, that accessibility is a real advantage.
Collaboration and sharing

Because Reecap lives in the browser and imports straight from Figma, it slots naturally into a modern design workflow where the source of truth is already a web tool. After Effects projects live in files on a specific machine with specific plugins, which can make handoff and collaboration heavier. Neither is wrong; they reflect different eras and philosophies of how creative work gets done.
The honest caveat about export

Fairness requires noting where Reecap is still maturing. After Effects exports to virtually any format with deep control over codecs and quality. In Reecap, the photo-to-video editor exports a polished MP4 today, but exporting a Motion Design project to video is still rolling out. So right now, Motion in Reecap is where you design and refine animations, and the video editor is where finished MP4s come from. If your only requirement is a rendered motion file this minute, factor that in. If your requirement is to design and iterate on motion quickly, Reecap is already excellent at that.
Which should you choose?

Choose After Effects when the work demands it: complex 3D, VFX, motion tracking, character animation, broadcast graphics, or frame-perfect control, and when you have the time, hardware, and budget to match. Choose Reecap when you want speed and simplicity: animating a Figma screen, building a social post, adding motion to a marketing card, or learning the craft without a wall of complexity in your way.

items: Pick After Effects for VFX, 3D, tracking, and broadcast work
Pick Reecap for UI animation, social posts, and product motion
Pick After Effects when you need deep export and codec control
Pick Reecap when speed, cost, and accessibility matter most

body.text: You can use both

These tools are not mutually exclusive. Many people will use Reecap for the fast 80 percent of jobs, quick animations, design previews, social content, and keep After Effects in their back pocket for the occasional project that genuinely needs its power. Using the lighter tool for light jobs frees up your time and energy for the rare work that actually justifies the heavyweight.
Performance, rendering, and waiting

There is a hidden cost in motion work that rarely makes the feature lists: waiting. After Effects previews can require RAM caching, and final output goes through a render queue that, for a heavy composition, can run for minutes or much longer while your machine is tied up. That is fine for a studio shipping a broadcast spot; it is friction for someone who just wants to see if a slide should be a touch slower. Reecap previews in real time in the browser, so the loop between a change and seeing the result is essentially instant. For iterative work, where you tweak, watch, tweak again, that immediacy is not a luxury; it is what keeps you in flow.

The flip side, stated plainly, is output control. After Effects can render virtually any format with fine control over codecs, bitrates, alpha channels, and color. Reecap's photo-to-video editor outputs a clean MP4 today, and Motion video export is still rolling out. So if your deliverable is a specific high-end render format right now, After Effects has the edge; if your deliverable is a fast, watchable result and quick iteration, Reecap removes the waiting entirely.
A note for teams and agencies

Tool choice is not only about the individual; it is about the team. After Effects expertise is a specialized skill, which means motion work tends to bottleneck on the one or two people who have it. A preset-based browser tool widens that bottleneck: a marketer, a social manager, or a junior designer can produce solid animated posts without pulling a motion specialist onto every small job. That frees your specialist for the work that genuinely needs their depth, and it lets the rest of the team move without waiting in a queue.

For agencies juggling many small deliverables, that division of labor is a real efficiency. Use the lightweight tool to clear the high-volume, low-complexity work fast, and reserve the heavyweight for the marquee projects that justify it. The result is more output, less bottleneck, and a happier specialist who is not spending their talent keyframing yet another simple lower-third.
The bottom line

After Effects is unmatched at the top end and will remain the professional standard for serious motion graphics. But power has a price in time, money, and complexity, and most everyday motion does not need to pay it. For animating designs, building social content, and learning motion fast, a browser tool like Reecap gets you to a strong result in a fraction of the time. The smart move is not loyalty to one tool; it is matching the tool to the task.

A useful way to decide on any given day is to ask one question: does this job need depth, or does it need speed? If the answer is depth, the kind of work where a frame-perfect curve or a complex 3D move genuinely matters, open After Effects and take the time it deserves. If the answer is speed, the far more common case of a social post, a product card, or a quick design animation, open a browser tab and have it done before the heavyweight would have finished launching. Most weeks are mostly speed jobs, which is precisely why a fast, accessible tool earns its place in a modern toolkit. Keep both, reach for the right one, and you will spend your time creating instead of fighting your software. And that, in the end, is the whole point of any tool: to disappear so the work can happen. Adobe's giant earns its complexity on the rare projects that truly need it, and a browser tool earns its place on the many everyday jobs that simply do not. Choose deliberately, project by project, rather than out of habit or loyalty, and neither tool will ever feel like a compromise. The goal was never to pick a side; it was to ship good motion with the least friction, and now you can.

faq.q: Is Reecap a real After Effects alternative?
faq.a: For everyday motion such as UI animation, social posts, and product graphics, yes. Reecap is faster and far easier to learn. For high-end VFX, 3D, and motion tracking, After Effects remains the right tool.

faq.q: Is Reecap free compared to After Effects?
faq.a: Yes. Reecap is free and open source, while After Effects is a paid Adobe Creative Cloud subscription billed monthly or annually.

faq.q: Can Reecap do everything After Effects can?
faq.a: No, and it does not try to. Reecap focuses on preset-based motion for designs, text, and shapes. After Effects has a far higher ceiling for complex compositing, 3D, and effects.

faq.q: Do I need a powerful computer for Reecap?
faq.a: No. Reecap runs in a browser and works well on modest laptops, whereas After Effects benefits from a powerful CPU, lots of RAM, and a strong GPU.

faq.q: Can Reecap export my motion project to video?
faq.a: The photo-to-video editor exports MP4s today. Exporting a Motion Design project to video is still rolling out, so for now Motion is where you design and refine animations.

title: Kinetic Typography: How to Animate Text That Grabs Attention
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Animated text is the workhorse of social video: captions, quotes, lyrics, hooks. This guide covers kinetic typography from first principles, and how to build it without keyframes.
description: A practical guide to kinetic typography and animated text. Learn the principles of readable text animation, common styles, timing for captions, and how to build it with presets in Reecap.

body.text: Kinetic typography is animated text, and it is everywhere for a reason. Scroll any social feed and you will see words sliding in, popping for emphasis, or revealing themselves to a beat. Animated text grabs attention, reinforces a message for the huge share of viewers who watch with the sound off, and gives an otherwise static design a pulse. This guide breaks down how to make text move well, the styles worth knowing, and how to build them quickly with presets instead of keyframes.

Text is the workhorse of social video. Captions, quotes, lyrics, hooks, and key stats are almost always typographic. Learn to animate text well and you have covered the majority of what motion design is actually used for day to day.
Why animated text works

Three forces make kinetic typography so effective. First, motion attracts the eye; a moving word wins attention over a still one almost every time. Second, most social video is watched muted, so on-screen text is often the only way your message lands. Third, animation can pace information, revealing one idea at a time so the viewer absorbs it instead of being hit with a wall of words. Good text animation is not decoration; it is communication.
Principle 1: Readability comes first

The cardinal rule of kinetic typography is that the viewer must be able to read it. An animation that looks cool but blurs past before anyone can parse the words has failed at its only job. That means three things in practice. Keep text on screen long enough to be read, which is roughly the time it takes to say it out loud plus a beat. Ensure strong contrast against the background. And avoid animations so busy that the letters are illegible while they move.

items: Hold text long enough to read it comfortably
Use high contrast between text and background
Avoid motion so intense the words are unreadable mid-animation
Prefer animating whole words or lines over individual letters for body copy

body.text: Principle 2: Match the energy to the message

The style of motion should fit the tone of the words. A soft fade suits an elegant quote or a calm brand. A punchy pop or a fast slide suits an energetic hook or a sale announcement. A bouncy entrance suits something playful and fun. When the motion and the message agree, the result feels intentional. When a gentle wellness quote arrives with an aggressive bounce, the mismatch is jarring even if the viewer cannot articulate why.
Principle 3: One idea at a time

The most powerful pattern in kinetic typography is sequencing. Rather than dropping a paragraph on screen at once, you reveal it phrase by phrase, each one entering as the last settles. This controls pace, builds anticipation, and keeps the viewer reading along at the rhythm you choose. It is the difference between handing someone a page and reading it to them with emphasis.
Common kinetic typography styles

A handful of styles cover most needs. The fade-in is the quiet classic, clean and unobtrusive, perfect when the words should be the star. The slide-in adds direction and momentum; sliding up reads as confident and is the most common choice for headlines. The pop scales a word up into place, ideal for emphasizing a single key term. The typewriter reveals characters one at a time, evoking conversation and great for hooks. And the blur-in resolves text from soft to sharp, which feels modern and premium.

items: Fade-in: clean and quiet, lets the words lead
Slide-up: confident and directional, the default for headlines
Pop: scales a key word into place for emphasis
Typewriter: characters appear one by one, conversational
Blur-in: resolves from soft to sharp for a premium feel

body.text: Timing animated captions to speech

If your text follows a voiceover or a song, timing is the whole game. The goal is for each phrase to appear in sync with when it is spoken or sung. A practical approach is to listen to the audio, note where each phrase lands, and set each text layer's start time to match. When a word pops exactly as it is said, the effect is deeply satisfying and feels professionally produced, even when it took only a few minutes to set up.

Even without audio, internal rhythm matters. Stagger your phrases so they enter at an even, musical cadence rather than randomly. The eye and ear both crave rhythm, and evenly spaced reveals feel composed.
Building kinetic type with presets

Here is the part that used to be tedious and no longer is. Traditionally, animating text meant keyframing position, opacity, and scale by hand for every word, then bending easing curves. With a preset-based tool like Reecap's Motion editor, you add a text layer, type your words, and choose an entrance preset such as slide-up or pop, with an easing like spring for bounce or ease-out for a clean settle. Set a start time and a duration, and the motion is generated for you. To sequence a phrase, duplicate the text layer for each line and stagger the start times. You get professional kinetic typography without a single keyframe.
A quick recipe: an animated quote

Let us build a shareable animated quote. Add a text layer for the first line of the quote and give it a slide-up entrance with ease-out. Add a second text layer for the next line, slide it up too, starting a beat later. Continue line by line, each entering after the last. Then add the attribution, the name of whoever said it, as a final small line that fades in once the quote is complete. Hold everything for a moment so it can be read, and you have a polished, sequenced quote card ready to post.

items: Line one: slide up with ease-out, starts first
Line two: slide up, starts a beat after line one
Continue for each line of the quote in sequence
Attribution: a small fade-in once the quote finishes
Hold the final state long enough to read before looping

body.text: Design choices that make text pop

Motion is only half of kinetic typography; the type itself matters. Use a clear, bold weight for short on-screen text; thin fonts vanish on small screens. Give text room to breathe with generous spacing. Consider a subtle background pill or a slight shadow behind text placed over busy imagery so it stays legible. And limit yourself to one or two typefaces and a tight color palette so the piece feels cohesive rather than chaotic.
Mistakes to avoid

A few errors show up constantly. Cramming too much text on screen at once overwhelms the viewer; reveal less, more often. Animating every individual letter of a long sentence turns reading into work; animate words or lines instead. Moving text so fast it cannot be read defeats the purpose; slow down and hold. And using a flashy effect that fights the message undermines the words; let the style serve the meaning.
Advanced kinetic techniques

Once the basics feel comfortable, a few advanced moves add real polish. Emphasis swaps are powerful: animate a whole phrase in calmly, then give one key word a second, distinct animation, a pop or a color change, so it stands out within the line. Layered timing, where a line slides up while a single word inside it scales, creates depth that a uniform entrance cannot. And combining motion with a subtle background element, a shape that wipes in behind the text, can frame the words and lift them off a busy image.

Another professional habit is designing the exit as carefully as the entrance. For looping clips you often hold the final state, but for sequenced pieces where one message replaces another, how text leaves matters as much as how it arrives. A quick fade or a slide in the opposite direction of the entrance keeps the transitions clean and stops old and new text from colliding. Thinking in full enter-hold-exit arcs, rather than just entrances, is what separates a string of effects from a composed sequence.

items: Emphasis swap: animate a phrase, then accent one key word
Layered timing: move a line while a word inside it scales
Framing: wipe a shape behind text to lift it off busy imagery
Designed exits: plan how text leaves, not just how it arrives

body.text: Accessibility and animated text

Animated captions are an accessibility win, since they carry your message to viewers who watch muted or who are hard of hearing, but motion can also work against accessibility if it is overdone. Keep contrast high, avoid rapid flashing or strobing effects that can be uncomfortable or harmful, and never sacrifice legibility for flair. The most accessible kinetic typography is also usually the most effective: clear, high-contrast, readable text that moves with purpose rather than for its own sake. Designing for the person who needs the text to be readable tends to make it better for everyone.
The takeaway

Kinetic typography is one of the highest-leverage skills in motion design because text is what most video needs to communicate. Keep it readable, match the energy to the message, reveal one idea at a time, and time your phrases to the rhythm or the audio. With preset-based animation, you can apply all of it in minutes. Master animated text and you have mastered the most-used corner of motion design.

The fastest way to improve is to make a lot of small pieces. Animate a quote a day for a week. Caption a clip with sequenced phrases. Take a headline you wrote and try it five different ways, fade, slide, pop, typewriter, blur, and notice how each one changes the feeling. Reps build instinct, and instinct is what lets you glance at a line of text and immediately know how it should move. Because preset-based tools strip away the tedium, you can do those reps in minutes instead of hours, which means you can actually build the habit. Animated text is a skill that compounds, and every small piece you finish makes the next one faster and better. The wonderful thing about animated text specifically is how directly the practice transfers: the same instincts that make a caption land also make a title sequence, a lyric video, or a kinetic quote sing. You are not learning six separate skills, you are learning one and applying it to different words. Put in a few focused reps this week, keep what works in a small mental library, and you will be surprised how quickly animating text goes from a thing you admire in other people's videos to a thing you simply do.

faq.q: What is kinetic typography?
faq.a: Kinetic typography is animated text. It is the practice of moving words on screen, sliding, fading, popping, or revealing them, to grab attention, pace information, and communicate even when video is muted.

faq.q: How do I make animated text without keyframes?
faq.a: Use a preset-based tool like Reecap's Motion editor. Add a text layer, type your words, and choose an entrance preset such as slide-up or pop with an easing, then set the start time and duration. No keyframes required.

faq.q: How long should animated text stay on screen?
faq.a: Long enough to read comfortably, roughly the time it takes to say the text out loud plus a short beat. Text that disappears too fast cannot do its job.

faq.q: What is the best animation style for headlines?
faq.a: A slide-up entrance with ease-out is the most reliable choice for headlines. It reads as confident and directional. Use pop to emphasize a single key word.

faq.q: How do I sync text to a voiceover or song?
faq.a: Note where each phrase lands in the audio, then set each text layer's start time to match, so words appear exactly as they are spoken or sung.

title: From Figma to Video: The Designer's Workflow for Animated Posts
author: Rakibul Islam
excerpt: Designers ship static frames all day, but feeds reward motion. Here is a repeatable workflow for turning your Figma designs into animated posts, from setup to a finished, on-brand clip.
description: A repeatable designer workflow for turning Figma designs into animated social posts. Learn how to structure frames for animation, import them into Reecap, and build on-brand motion fast.

body.text: Designers produce static frames all day: feature cards, launch announcements, quote graphics, app screens, promo banners. Social feeds, meanwhile, reward motion. A still image is easy to scroll past; a moving one earns a half-second of attention, and half a second is often all you need. The gap between what designers make and what feeds want is exactly where a Figma-to-video workflow pays off. This guide lays out a repeatable process for turning your existing designs into animated posts without rebuilding them in a separate tool.

The key insight is that you have already done the hard part. The layout, the hierarchy, the color, the type, it all exists in your Figma file. Animation is the final, fast layer on top. With the right workflow, you can take a design you finished an hour ago and have an animated version posted before lunch.
Design frames with animation in mind

The smoothest motion starts in Figma, before you ever think about animating. When a frame is well structured, it animates beautifully; when it is a flat soup of ungrouped elements, it fights you. Two habits make all the difference. First, group related elements: a card and its contents, a headline and its underline, an icon and its label. Groups become movable units you can animate together. Second, build a clear visual hierarchy, because the order things should animate in is almost always the order the eye should read them.

items: Group related elements so they animate as one unit
Build a clear hierarchy that doubles as your animation order
Keep important text as real text, not outlined or rasterized
Use solid fills where you can, since they stay editable on import

body.text: The core workflow, step by step

Once a frame is structured, the workflow is short and repeatable. You copy the frame from Figma with the Reecap plugin, paste it into Reecap's Motion tool, animate the layers with presets, refine the timing on the timeline, and you have an animated post. The first time it might take fifteen minutes as you learn the layout; after that it is a five-minute task. Let us walk through each step as a routine you can internalize.
Step 1: Copy the frame from Figma

With the Reecap Motion plugin installed in your Figma desktop app, select the frame you want to animate and run the plugin. It previews your frame and offers a Copy to Reecap button. Click it, and your design is on the clipboard as an editable layer tree, not a screenshot. Text stays text, solid shapes stay shapes, groups stay groups, and anything too complex to represent natively comes across as a flattened image so it still looks right.
Step 2: Paste into Reecap

Open Reecap, switch to the Motion tool, and paste onto the canvas. Your frame appears exactly as designed, sized to match, with its background color intact, and tucked into a single collapsed group in the layers panel so the list stays clean. Expand it to reach the layers inside. Because everything imports static and visible, you can confirm it looks right before adding any motion.
Step 3: Animate from the bottom up

Animate in reading order, which usually means bottom of the stack to top of the attention hierarchy. Bring the background card or container in first with a gentle scale or fade. Then the headline with a confident slide-up. Then supporting text a beat later. Then the call to action with a tactile pop. Then any decorative accent last, as a flourish. Stagger the start times so the elements cascade rather than firing at once, and lean on easing, ease-out for entrances, spring for buttons, to keep everything feeling natural.

items: Container or background: scale or fade in first
Headline: slide up, a beat later
Body or supporting text: slide up or fade, after the headline
Call to action: pop with spring easing
Accent or icon: arrives last as a flourish

body.text: Step 4: Refine on the timeline

The timeline turns a decent animation into a polished one. Each layer is a clip you can drag to change when it starts and resize to change how long it is on screen. Zoom in for precise adjustments or fit the whole composition to see the rhythm at a glance. Scrub the playhead to inspect any single frame, and play it back repeatedly, tuning the stagger until the entrances feel musical. This iterative pass is short but it is where craft lives.
Step 5: Keep it on brand

Because the layers are editable, brand consistency is easy to enforce in place. Recolor a shape to your exact brand value, adjust the frame background, rewrite or resize text, all without returning to Figma. Build a small mental library of motion that fits your brand, the same entrance style, the same easing, the same pacing, and reuse it across posts. Consistent motion is a powerful, underused brand signal; when your animations all share a feel, your feed looks designed.
Turning one design into many posts

A single workflow unlocks volume. Once you have an animated template feel, you can swap the content and produce a series quickly: the same animated card structure with new headlines for a multi-part announcement, the same quote-card motion with different quotes, the same feature-highlight animation for each feature you ship. The motion becomes a reusable pattern and the content becomes the variable. This is how design teams keep a feed full without animating from scratch every time.
Practical tips that save time

A few habits compound. Name your layers in Figma; clear names survive the import and make the layers panel far easier to navigate. Keep critical type as editable text so it stays crisp and changeable. Use groups generously, since group-level animation is the fastest way to move a whole section cohesively. And decide your animation order before you start applying presets, so you are executing a plan rather than improvising.

items: Name layers in Figma so they read clearly after import
Keep important type as editable text
Group sections to animate them in one move
Plan the animation order before applying any preset
Reuse a consistent motion style as a brand signal

body.text: Know the current limits

Set expectations so nothing trips you up. Custom Figma fonts fall back to a system font in the browser, though size, weight, color, alignment, and the text itself transfer. Complex vectors, icons, and effects come in as flattened images, which look correct but are not vector-editable. And exporting a Motion project to a video file is still rolling out, so today Motion is where you design and refine, while the photo-to-video editor is where finished MP4s come from. For iterating on design motion and previewing animated posts, the workflow is already fast and reliable.
Building a reusable motion system

The biggest long-term win is not any single animated post; it is a motion system you reuse. Just as you maintain a design system of colors, type, and components in Figma, you can maintain a small motion system: a standard entrance for headlines, a standard easing for the whole brand, a standard pace for reveals, a standard treatment for calls to action. Once that system exists in your head and your habits, every new post is faster and the whole feed gains a consistent, recognizable feel. Viewers may never consciously notice it, but consistency is exactly what makes content read as professional rather than ad hoc.

Document your motion system the same way you document your design system. Write down the defaults: headlines slide up with ease-out over 0.6 seconds, buttons pop with spring, sections stagger by 0.15 seconds. Share it with whoever else makes content. Now anyone on the team can produce on-brand motion without guessing, and your animated posts stop looking like they came from different sources. A motion system turns one person's good instincts into a repeatable team capability.

items: Define a default entrance and easing for the brand
Set a standard stagger interval and a standard hold time
Decide a consistent treatment for calls to action
Write it down and share it so the whole team can reuse it

body.text: Your first week with the workflow

If you are starting from zero, here is a gentle ramp. On day one, just import one finished Figma frame and animate it with a single entrance per layer; do not aim for perfection, aim for familiarity with the copy-paste-animate loop. Over the next few days, animate a few more frames and start paying attention to your timing, nudging start times until the cascades feel right. A week of small reps is enough to make this a comfortable, five-minute routine rather than a project.
The bottom line

Designers already create everything a great animated post needs; the missing piece is a fast bridge from static to motion. Structure your frames with groups and hierarchy, copy them into Reecap with the Figma plugin, animate from the bottom up with staggered presets, and refine on the timeline. faq.q: How do I turn a Figma design into a video?
faq.a: Use the Reecap Motion Figma plugin to copy a frame, paste it into Reecap's Motion tool as editable layers, animate each layer with presets, and refine the timing on the timeline.

faq.q: How should I structure Figma frames for animation?
faq.a: Group related elements so they animate together, build a clear visual hierarchy that doubles as your animation order, keep important text as real text, and prefer solid fills, which stay editable on import.

faq.q: In what order should I animate elements?
faq.a: Animate in reading order: container or background first, then headline, then supporting text, then the call to action, then any accent. Stagger the start times so they cascade.

faq.q: Can I keep my designs on brand when animating?
faq.a: Yes. Because layers import as editable, you can recolor shapes, change the frame background, and edit text directly in Reecap. Reusing a consistent motion style also reinforces your brand.

faq.q: Can I export the animation as a video file?
faq.a: Exporting a Motion project to video is still rolling out. Today, Motion is where you design and preview animations, while the photo-to-video editor exports finished MP4s.
